This handles several edge cases:

* `low` or `high` is NaN. In this case, `scale` and `res` will be NaN.
* `low` is negative infinity and `high` is finite. `scale` will be infinite, and `res` will be NaN.
* `high` is positive infinity and `low` is finite. `scale` will be infinite, and `res` will be infinite or NaN (if `value0_1` is 0).
* `low` is negative infinity and `high` is positive infinity. `scale` will be infinite, and `res` will be NaN.
* `low` and `high` are finite, but `high - low` overflows to infinity. `scale` will be infinite, and `res` will be infinite or NaN (if `value0_1` is 0).

Therefore, if `high` or `low` is non-finite, the `res < high` check above is guaranteed to fail, and execution will end up here.

The handler type has already been resolved, so the instantiator is responsible only for providing a configured instance. It may construct and configure a new instance or recycle a shared instance. One use case is enabling dependency injection, which would otherwise be difficult to implement.

Custom instances may return `null` to indicate that the caller should use the default instantiation process: calling the no-argument constructor through reflection.

Care must be taken to ensure that any shared instance returned is thread-safe. The caller will not synchronize access to returned instances, so custom instances must provide their own thread safety when shared.
